title: Ownership, control & cash claims
transcript:
PAGE 1
Shareholders: Elect the board -> Board: Appoints / monitors CEO -> Managers: Run operations
Governance flow: ownership and day-to-day control are separate.
A. Alder Tools - distribution worksheet
Pretax corporate earnings | $1,000.00
Assumed corporate tax rate | 20%
Payout policy | Distribute all after-corporate-tax earnings
Shares outstanding | 100 identical shares
Maya owns | 10 shares
Assumed dividend tax rate | 25%
Hypothetical C corporation; no other taxes, fees, or deductions. Calculate corporate tax first, then the dividend tax on the amount actually distributed. Rates are exercise assumptions, not current tax rules.

B. Claims and funding map
Equity | Residual claim after creditors; dividends are discretionary
Debt | Contractual payments; default may transfer control
New share issue | Investor cash flows to the issuing company
Investor resale | Buyer cash flows to the selling investor
Assume no personal guarantees. Limited liability protects personal assets; it does not protect the amount invested in shares.

PAGE 2
Investor buys: Pays dealer ASK -> Dealer quotes: Bid $20.00 / Ask $20.40 -> Investor sells: Receives dealer BID
C. Unchanged quote; sufficient depth for 25 shares; no commission or other fees.
C. Trade ticket
Order size | 25 shares
Bid per share | $20.00
Ask per share | $20.40
An immediate purchase and resale uses the ask first and the bid second. The company issues no new shares in this trade.

D. Fresh distribution case - Birch Works
Pretax earnings | $2,000.00
Assumed corporate tax rate | 25%
Payout policy | Distribute all after-corporate-tax earnings
Maya ownership | 20% of identical shares
Assumed personal dividend tax rate | 20%
Calculate the total taxes across the company and all shareholders, or Maya's personal cash, as requested. No other taxes or deductions.

E. Decision memo
Proposal A | A project raises long-run firm value
Proposal B | A prestige office benefits the CEO but lowers firm value
Social spillover | Neither proposal's private cash flows price every effect on outsiders
Evaluate owner-manager incentives separately from effects on society. Bankruptcy reorganization may preserve a viable operating business.

title: Alder Tools - linked financial statements
transcript:
PAGE 1
Balance sheet: Position at a date -> Income statement: Earnings over a year -> Cash flow statement: Reconcile cash change
All amounts are dollars, not thousands. Parentheses indicate outflows or deductions.
A. Comparative balance sheet
Account | Beginning of year | End of year
Cash | 1,000 | To calculate
Accounts receivable | 800 | 1,000
Inventory | 1,200 | 1,500
Net property, plant & equipment | 5,000 | 5,300
Total assets | 8,000 | 9,500
Accounts payable | 1,000 | 1,100
Interest-bearing debt | 2,500 | 3,000
Book equity | 4,500 | To calculate
All debt is long-term. Accounts payable is the only current liability. No other assets, liabilities, or equity adjustments. Use ending balances for ratios unless the prompt says otherwise.

B. Income statement - year ended
Sales | 10,000
Cost of goods sold | (6,000)
Cash operating expenses | (1,500)
Depreciation | (500)
Interest expense | (400)
Income tax | (400)
No other income or expense. Gross profit, EBIT, pretax income, and net income are deliberately omitted. Assumed tax rate: 25% of positive pretax income.

PAGE 2
Start with net income -> Adjust noncash items: and working capital -> Add investing: and financing flows
C. Indirect cash-flow reconciliation: use changes, not ending balances.
C. Cash movements and supporting notes
Capital expenditure paid in cash | 800
New borrowing received in cash | 500
Dividends paid in cash | 300
Share issues / repurchases | None
Other noncash items / cash flows | None
Operating cash flow = net income + depreciation - increase in receivables - increase in inventory + increase in payables. Investing cash flow includes the equipment purchase. Financing cash flow includes the borrowing and dividends.

D. Market and per-share information
Common shares throughout the year | 1,000
Current price per share | $8.00
Total debt at year end | $3,000.00
Cash at year end | Reconcile using panels A-C
For enterprise value use debt at its stated value and subtract all cash. No preferred shares or minority interests. This is a separate scale example from Chapter 1.

E. Analyst reference
Current assets | Cash + receivables + inventory
Quick assets | Cash + receivables (no other liquid securities)
Profitability | Gross profit, EBIT, or net income divided by sales
DuPont ROE | Net margin x sales/assets x assets/book equity
Collection / inventory days | Receivables/daily sales; inventory/daily cost of sales
Use 365 days for daily rates. Notes and audit opinions help assess accounting estimates and risk; a clean opinion does not guarantee the business will succeed.

title: Market values, replication & NPV
transcript:
PAGE 1
Today (t=0): Value costs / benefits -> Bank exchange rate: 10% for one year -> Year 1 (t=1): Value costs / benefits
Certain dollar cash flows. Borrowing and lending both available at 10% unless a panel states otherwise.
A. Same-day materials offer
Delivery | 12 standardized units today
Competitive resale price | $50.00 per unit
Purchase cost today | $500.00
Purchase and sale are simultaneous. No transport costs, bid-ask spread, or quantity constraints. The buyer can resell every unit.

B. Bank and security quotes
Reference bank deposit today | $1,000.00
One-year bank rate | 10%
Bond certain payoff at t=1 | $1,100.00
Quoted bond price today | $980.00
Separate certain receipt at t=1 | $1,210.00
The bond and bank repayment have identical date, currency, and default risk. Borrowing is available to fund the bond purchase. Ignore trading costs and collateral restrictions.

C. Risk-state illustration
Claim | Weak economy | Strong economy
A | 0 | 200
B | 200 | 0
Each state is equally likely. A and B have the same average payout, but their payouts occur in different economic states. Do not assume their prices are equal.

PAGE 2
t=0: Machine cost $900 -> t=1: Receipt $1,210 -> t=1: Service outlay $110
D. The receipt and service outlay happen on the same future date. All are certain.
D. Machine proposal
Initial equipment payment at t=0 | $900.00
Receipt at t=1 | $1,210.00
Required service payment at t=1 | $110.00
Matched annual discount rate | 10%
Other flows, taxes, transaction costs | None
Value every cost and benefit on one date. The service payment must be included even though it occurs after the purchase. Evaluate this project independently; it is not a choice between mutually exclusive projects.

E. Replication ledger - blank working copy
Position | Today | Year 1
Buy the bond from B | Pay quoted price | Receive $1,100
Borrow against its payoff | Receive loan principal | Repay $1,100
Combined position | Calculate net cash | Compare the two flows
Borrow exactly the present value of the future repayment. An arbitrage requires no negative future net payoff and a positive payoff somewhere, after costs. A merely optimistic forecast is not arbitrage.

F. Transaction cost variation
Buy one identical claim | Ask $101
Sell one identical claim | Bid $100
Observation | Last traded prices may differ from executable prices
Compare actual buying and selling prices, including fees. Without an executable profit, a displayed price discrepancy is not an arbitrage opportunity.

title: Cash-flow timelines & delayed payments
transcript:
PAGE 1
t=0: Deposit $1,000 -> t=1: No withdrawal -> t=2: Receive ending balance
A. A single deposit earns 10% per year with annual compounding; no tax or fees.
A. Deposit / discounting
Starting deposit at t=0 | $1,000.00
Annual effective rate | 10%
Separate certain receipt at t=2 | $1,210.00
The deposit is made once. Distinguish the ending balance from interest earned.

B. Two-payment contract
Payment received at t=1 | $121.00
Payment received at t=2 | $121.00
Annual effective rate | 10%
No payment today. These are equal end-of-year payments. Value each cash flow at t=0 before combining them.

C. Endowment promise
Level annual payment | $50.00
First payment | One year from today
Last payment | None; payments continue forever
Discount rate | 5% per year
Separate growth variation: first payment C1, growth rate g, discount rate r. The infinite growing-stream formula requires r > g. The level-payment case has g = 0.

PAGE 2
t=0: Pay $150 -> t=2: Valuation anchor -> t=3: Receive $121 -> t=4: Receive $121
D. Delayed contract. Annual effective discount rate: 10%. No other cash flows.
D. Delayed contract inputs
Initial purchase price at t=0 | $150.00
First receipt at t=3 | $121.00
Second and final receipt at t=4 | $121.00
Effective rate per year | 10%
The ordinary-annuity formula values the receipts one period before the first payment, at t=2. Move that value back two more periods to today. Keep full precision until the final cent.

E. Timing and payment reference
Ordinary annuity | Equal payments at dates 1 through N
Annuity due | Equal payments at dates 0 through N-1
Payment on an amortizing loan | Principal / ordinary-annuity PV factor
Future savings goal | Target future value / ordinary-annuity FV factor
IRR | Rate making the signed cash-flow NPV zero
Cash-flow signs depend on whose perspective is used. A loan is positive at origination for the borrower and negative during repayment.

F. Tool and growth checks
Spreadsheet NPV(rate, future flows) | Discounts its first listed flow by one period
Cash flow today | Add separately; it is not discounted
Rate per period | Must match the spacing of payments
Finite growing stream | Can be discounted term by term even when g >= r
A calculator is optional. Multiplication, division, and a two-payment timeline are enough for the numerical koans in this chapter.

title: Rate quotes, loan ledger & purchasing power
transcript:
PAGE 1
Quote: 12% APR -> Semiannual rate: APR / 2 -> One year: Two compounding periods
A. Rate quotes describe a convention; convert to an effective rate for the cash-flow period.
A. Savings quote
Deposit today | $1,000.00
Quoted APR | 12%
Compounding | Semiannual (twice per year)
Withdrawals, tax, fees | None
Compute a half-year balance first, then a full-year balance. Reinvest all interest. APR and EAR coincide only when compounding is annual (or the rate is zero).

B. Loan statement
Opening principal before month 1 | $2,000.00
Quoted APR | 12%, compounded monthly
Scheduled month-end payment | $220.00
Extra payment in month 1 | None
Extra payment in month 2 | $100.00 after the scheduled payment
Fees or penalties | None
Monthly rate = APR / 12. Interest accrues on the opening balance. Each scheduled payment first covers that month's interest; its remainder reduces principal. The extra month-2 payment reduces principal immediately.

C. Borrower decision note
Outstanding balance | PV of remaining contractual payments at the loan rate
Refinance comparison | Include fees, remaining term, and all changed payments
Teaser rate | An initial rate may reset later
A lower monthly payment alone does not establish a lower financing cost; a longer repayment term may explain the reduction.

PAGE 2
1-year spot: 4% annual effective -> 2-year spot: 5% annual effective -> 3-year spot: 6% annual effective
D. Illustrative upward-sloping spot curve; each quote applies to its entire maturity.
D. Spot-rate valuation
Payment in one year | Discount by 1.04
Payment in two years | Discount by 1.05 squared
Payment in three years | Discount by 1.06 cubed
These are annualized zero-coupon spot rates, not sequential one-year rates. A flat-rate annuity shortcut does not apply directly to this nonflat curve. This is an illustration, not a current market quote.

E. After-tax purchasing-power case
Deposit today | $1,000.00
Nominal effective annual interest rate | 10%
Tax rate on interest only | 20%, paid at year end
Inflation over the year | 8%
Principal tax, fees, other flows | None
Compute gross interest, tax on that interest, after-tax ending dollars, then divide by the inflation factor to express the result in today's purchasing power. Carry full precision until the end.

F. Discount-rate matching
Cash-flow attributes | Currency, date, risk, nominal/real, before/after tax
Opportunity cost | Expected return on a comparable-risk, comparable-term alternative
Promised risky yield | May exceed expected return because of default losses
Interest tax deduction | Use only when explicitly assumed usable
A risky portfolio's expected return is not a suitable discount rate for a guaranteed liability merely because the portfolio is intended to fund it. Retained cash also has an opportunity cost.
